1:
Gill states three uses for the list. It shows the original of the several nations, from whom they sprang and by whom they were founded; it confutes the pretended antiquity of the Egyptians, Chaldeans and Chinese; and it points out the people who were to be the seat of the church for many ages and from whom the Messiah should spring, which Gill takes for the principal view of the history. Keil and Delitzsch pair the chapter with the next: the genealogy traces the origin of the tribes scattered over the earth, and the confusion of tongues gives the cause of the division of one race into many with languages of their own. They then defend the record. It is not an ethnographical myth, nor an ancient Hebrew's attempt to connect his own people with the rest of the world by uncertain traditions and subjective combinations, but a historical account of the genesis of the nations, resting on a tradition from the fathers which, to judge by its contents, belongs to the age of Abraham. Ellicott adds only that Shem, Ham and Japheth stand in that undeviating order throughout.

Henry asks why Japheth is treated first and offers two answers: he was the eldest, or his family lay remotest from Israel and had least to do with them. That race is dispatched briefly, since Moses hastens on to Ham, Israel's enemies, and Shem, Israel's ancestors; for it is the church that Scripture is designed to be the history of, and the nations only so far as they bore on Israel's affairs. Henry marks that the sons were born after the flood, to rebuild the world of mankind the flood had ruined: he that had killed now makes alive. On the isles of the Gentiles he allows himself a guess and a hope. The allotment was made by lot after a survey, and probably this island of ours was in it; since all places beyond the sea from Judea are called isles, he reads the promise that the isles shall wait for his law of the conversion of the Gentiles. But he sets a limit. No nation except the Jews can be sure which of these seventy it came from, the lists having been kept among them alone for the sake of the Messiah, though learned men have shown with some probability which nations descended from each brother.

Clarke's caution is the sharpest note in the passage. It is extremely difficult to say what peoples sprang from the three grand divisions, since most of these names have changed in the long lapse from the deluge to the Christian era, though a few are distinctly marked. His main point is that Moses names not the first settler but the people from whom the country afterwards took its name. Mizraim is a dual and could never have been a man's name, and the same holds of Kittim, Dodanim, Ludim, Philistim and Caphtorim, which are plurals. Among Canaan's posterity whole nations stand in place of the men they sprang from, the Jebusite, Amorite and Girgasite; and Moses even enters names of places remarkable in the sacred history instead of settlers, as elsewhere Salma is called the father of Bethlehem and Joab the father of the valley of craftsmen. Clarke also passes on, without vouching for it, the report that Noah was commanded to make a will bequeathing the East to Shem, Africa to Ham, and Europe with its isles to Japheth. Calvin declines the enquiry, saying he does not condemn the industry of those who pursue it and will let them enjoy the reward of their labours. What interests him is that in these bare names we still hold a fragment of the world's history, and that so many forgot it; the memory of the deluge was lost by most, opening the door to the fables of the heathen poets.
2:
Gill observes that Japheth, named last, is treated first, by the figure rhetoricians call a chiasm, and reports from Josephus that his sons settled from Taurus and Amanus eastward to the Tanais and westward to Gadira. Of the seven, Gomer draws the most comment. Gill has him father the Gomerites whom the Greeks of Josephus's day called Galatians, the Gauls of Asia Minor who held Phrygia, both names signifying the same on Bochart's showing, the country looking as though scorched. Clarke identifies Japheth with the Japetus of the Greeks, gives Magog to the Scythians and Tartars, on the strength of names in great Tartary that still echo Gog and Magog, and grants Javan to the Ionians, Tiras to the Thracians, Tubal to the Iberians and Meshech to the Cappadocians. On Madai he balks: the Medes are the usual answer, but Joseph Mede makes it probable that the founder of the Macedonian Maedi is meant, and concludes that nothing certain can be advanced. Ellicott is bolder. Gomer reappears in the Cimmerians, who left their name in the Crimea before a branch struck across Russia and skirted the Baltic to become the Cimbri of Denmark and Cymry of Wales; Magog is the Scythians, represented now by the Russians; and since the Getae were Thracians and ancestors of the Goths, Tiras ends in Scandinavia.

Gomer's sons expose how little of this is settled. On Ashkenaz, Keil and Delitzsch canvass the old Jewish explanation that the Germani are meant, and Knobel's derivation from a family of Asi supported by the German legend of Mannus, but report that Kiepert and Bochart decide on geographical grounds for the Ascanians of northern Phrygia. Ellicott places the region near Armenia and thinks the race wandered thence into Germany, admitting the derivations are all most uncertain while judging the Jews probably right to call Germans Ashkenazites. Clarke suggests the Armenian province of Sacagena and notes Pliny's Ascanitici about the Tanais. Riphath fares no better: Keil gives Knobel's Celts, who crossed the Rhipaean mountains toward the Northern Ocean, against Josephus and Kiepert for Paphlagonia, and calls both very uncertain; Clarke takes the Paphlagonians, anciently the Riphataei; Ellicott prefers the men of the Rhipaean mountains, whom he also makes Celts. Only Togarmah commands agreement, Keil noting the Armenians still call themselves the house of Thorgom, Ellicott saying flatly it is certainly Armenia. Ellicott closes with a remark on what the chapter leaves out: the extension of Japheth eastward was as remarkable as westward, Parthia, Bactria and India being as Japhethite as Germany, Greece and Rome.

Javan's sons run the same course. Tarshish divides them more sharply. Keil holds to the Spanish colony of Tartessus, reporting Knobel's Etruscans and Delitzsch's objection that these were probably of Lydian and so Shemite descent; Clarke makes it Cilicia, whose capital was the Tarsus where Paul was born; Ellicott thinks Tartessus too late here and prefers the Tyrseni, powerful in Italy, Corsica and Sardinia, who he supposes founded Tartessus and named it. On Dodanim both Clarke and Ellicott note the reading is doubtful, the Hebrew letters for R and D being so alike that Rodanim stands in Chronicles and several versions; Clarke offers Dodona, Rhodes or the Rhone, Ellicott says no dependence can be placed on the reading and takes the Rodanim for Rhodians. On the isles Gill argues the word cannot mean islands proper, which would not have held Japheth's posterity, and which men would hardly have sought when shipping was little known; the Hebrews called all places reached by sea or lying on the coast islands, so the phrase is better rendered the countries of the Gentiles. Ellicott presses further, that as there were no Gentiles yet the words mean the coast-lands of the nations, and Keil confines them to the Mediterranean shore from Asia Minor to Spain. Wesley keeps only that the allotment was made by lot after a survey.
6:
Ellicott reports the popular derivation of Ham from a root meaning sunburnt, paired with a root for fair behind Japheth, so that the brothers father dark, fair and olive-coloured races; he prefers Chemi, the old name of Egypt, from the black colour of its soil. Keil and Delitzsch arrive at the same place from the other end, noting that the old Egyptian Kemi was traced by Plutarch to the dark ash-grey silt of the Nile but is more correctly traced to Ham. Both make Cush the Ethiopians of the ancients, and both deny the name was African originally: Keil has the Cushites scattered over southern Asia and settled originally in Arabia, where those who stayed took a Shemitic language, while Ellicott puts their home on the Tigris and Euphrates, where Nimrod raised them to power, before they spread into Arabia and crossed the Red Sea into Nubia. Keil takes the dual Mizraim for Upper and Lower Egypt and calls the name untraceable to any Semitic root; Ellicott agrees it may be such a dual but thinks it safer to leave the word until knowledge increases, adding that Brugsch-Bey, from the skulls of many mummies, concluded the ancient Egyptians were no African race but Caucasian, of a Cushite branch, cradled in Central Asia. Clarke keeps to a line apiece; Gill quotes Josephus that Ham's sons held from Syria and the mountains to the sea, and adds that many names are lost and others so bent into other tongues as to be scarcely recognisable.

Cush's sons are placed with more confidence than Japheth's. Keil finds Seba at Meroe, Havilah among the Macrobian Ethiopians, Sabtah in Hadhramaut, Raamah at a bay in south-eastern Arabia and Sabtecah in Caramania, with Raamah's sons Sheba and Dedan near the Persian Gulf, whence the Sabaean and Dedanitic Cushites spread north-west into mixed tribes with the children of Joktan and Abraham. Ellicott draws the implicit conclusion: when this table was written the southern half of Arabia was Cushite, and a race far darker than the light brown Arabians is still found in Yemen and Hadramaut; but their chief home then was Mesopotamia, where the cuneiform inscriptions have now disclosed their long struggle with men of the race of Shem.

Nimrod divides the commentators as no other name here does. Henry and Wesley take him for a tyrant in the making: those before him were content to stand level with their neighbours, but his aspiring mind would lord it over them, the spirit of the giants before the flood reviving in him so soon after that judgment. His hunting they read two ways, either that he rid the country of wild beasts and so won his neighbours' affection, or that under that pretence he gathered armed men and became a violent invader of their rights; he thought himself a mighty prince, but before the Lord he was only a mighty hunter, and great conquerors, Henry adds, are but great hunters, Alexander appearing in prophecy as no more than a he-goat pushing. Calvin sets him against the moderation of his age, when men of dignity governed by civil laws and had more authority than power, and finds him branded with an eternal mark of infamy, from which we learn how pleasing to God a mild administration is. Clarke derives the name from a root meaning to rebel and piles up the Targums, which make him a hunter of men and a rebel before the Lord; Keil reads the Greek as against Jehovah rather than before him. Ellicott alone defends him. Explaining Hamite names by Hebrew roots he calls unscholarlike; the narrative speaks rather in Nimrod's commendation, and the traditions blackening him date only from Josephus. On his reading Nimrod was a public benefactor who organised the hunt and then undertook the harder work of bringing order among men who had lived in scattered groups with no means of punishing violence.
10:
Gill defends Nimrod's title to Babel against the classical writers who gave it to Semiramis or Ninus. The truest account, he says, makes Belus the builder, and Belus is Nimrod; Curtius allows that most believe so, Berosus blames the Greeks for crediting Semiramis, and Abydenus reports that Belus walled it. Gill draws a chronological conclusion: the whole notice of Nimrod is written by anticipation, since he was no powerful prince until after Babel was built and the languages confounded. Clarke observes that the name means confusion, a proper one for a kingdom founded in apostasy and supported by tyranny and rapine. Ellicott dissents on the etymology while agreeing about the man. Babel is Bab-ili, the gate of God, a literal Assyrian rendering of the older Accadian name; the derivation from a root for confusion belongs to the next chapter and is derisive. He identifies Shinar with Babylonia, the lower part of Mesopotamia against Assyria the upper, called Sumir in the inscriptions and named the land of Nimrod by Micah; and he brings Erech into the light of the tablets as Urak, the great southern city of the Izdubar legends, ravaged by an Elamite king, now Warka, and supposed from its mounds and coffins to have been an early royal burial place.

Calvin will not have Babylon made as grand as the profane historians do. He grants that Moses names the seat of the empire and four cities subject to it, though whether Nimrod founded them or drove out their lords he leaves open, and suspects the region's fruitfulness invited later hands to enlarge the place, until Aristotle took it out of the rank of cities and compared it to a province. That, he thinks, is how the work came to be ascribed to Semiramis, whom others credit only with adorning and bridging it; and he takes the land of Shinar for a note of discrimination, since there was another Babylon in Egypt, now Cairo. Wesley reads the verse for what it shows about government, not masonry. Nimrod some way got into power and laid the foundation of a monarchy afterwards a head of gold; he had no apparent right to rule by birth, so either his fitness recommended him or power and policy advanced him into the throne. He takes this for the antiquity of civil government, and of that form which lodges sovereignty in a single person.

The eleventh verse turns on one word. Gill lays the question out: is Asshur a man's name or a country's? Read as a country, the sentence says that out of that land he went forth into Assyria, and Gill lists Onkelos, Junius, Piscator and Bochart for it, with the margin of the English Bible; the Targum of Jonathan is express that Nimrod went, having refused the counsel of the generation of the division, and Theophilus says the same. Gill notes that most who take this route give a better reason than the Targumist, that Nimrod, not content with his own dominions, made war on Assyria and seized it. Clarke prefers the marginal reading outright, adds that Assyria is therefore called the land of Nimrod, and thinks Ninus, from whom Nineveh is supposedly named, probably Nimrod himself; of Rehoboth and Calah nothing certain is known. Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way and make the four places one composite city carrying the name of Nineveh, so that the great city at the end describes Nineveh rather than Resen. Calvin alone reports the other side with sympathy: Asshur may well have been of the posterity of Shem, and the received opinion is that he is named because Nimrod violently expelled him, which would mark the tyrant's ferocity. Such, he adds, are the fruits of a greatness that keeps within no bounds, whence the old proverb that great kingdoms are great robberies. Yet he too adopts the reading that makes Asshur a country.
13:
Every name in Mizraim's line is a plural, and Gill takes the point first: Ludim is not a man but a people, so Mizraim begat the father of the Ludim. He identifies them with the Lydians, distinguished from the Lydians of Asia Minor who came from Lud the son of Shem, and follows Bochart in placing them in Africa as the Ethiopians now called Abyssines, once famous for archery; anyone reading Diodorus Siculus, he adds, will see the likeness between Egyptians and Ethiopians, who deified their kings alike, took the same care over funerals and used hieroglyphics. Clarke works through the rest in a line apiece. Ludim he puts in the Mareotis, Anamim about the temple of Jupiter Ammon, Lehabim among the Libyans west of the Thebaid, and Casluhim in Colchis, which almost all authors allow was peopled from Egypt; of Naphtuhim even conjecture can scarcely fix a place, though Bochart inclines to Marmarica, and Caphtorim he gives to Cyprus after Calmet. On Pathrusim both prefer Bochart's Thebaid, the upper Egypt called Pathros in Scripture, Clarke noting that the Chaldee paraphrase puts them in the Delta, and Gill setting aside Hillerus, who compounds the word into a corner of the Rosians at the bay of Issus.

With Canaan's line the interest shifts from geography to grammar. Keil and Delitzsch argue that Zidon here is a man, not the Phoenician capital. The apposition his firstborn and the verb begat both require a person; a city name would not harmonise with the other descendants, whose analogy calls for the gentile form Sidonian; and the word, from a root meaning to hunt, does not suit a seaport, so there are serious philological objections to Justin's derivation of it from the plenty of fish on that coast. Heth they take the same way, a person from whom the Hittites are named. Gill reaches the same verdict by the shorter road, granting Justin's derivation but holding that since Canaan had a son of the name, the city was no doubt called from him; he adds that Sidon is older than Tyre, which the Sidonians built, and that Homer mentions the one and not the other. Of the peoples that follow, Gill notes that the Jebusites gave Jerusalem its older name of Jebus and held it so strongly that Judah could not drive them out until David, and that Bochart thought their name survived on the island once called Ebusus. The Hivites he places in Hermon, and passes on the guess that their name means dwellers in caves like serpents, which is why Cadmus the Phoenician and his wife are fabled to have been turned into serpents.

Henry asks why Canaan's posterity is described more particularly than any other family here, and answers that these were the nations to be subdued before Israel, whose land was in time to become the holy land, Immanuel's land. God had an eye to that, he says, when he cast the lot of this devoted race in the very spot he had chosen for his own people, which is what Moses means when the Most High, dividing to the nations their inheritance, set the bounds of the people by the number of the children of Israel. The second thing Henry draws out is harder. By this account Canaan's posterity were numerous, rich and pleasantly situated, and yet Canaan lay under a divine curse, and not a curse causeless. Those under the curse of God may still prosper greatly in this world, for we cannot know love or hatred by what is before us but by what is within us; the curse always works really and terribly, but it may work secretly. Wesley states the same thing as a comparison and leaves it there: Canaan has here a better land than either Shem or Japheth, and yet they have the better lot, for they inherit the blessing.
21:
Calvin notices that Shem alone is given a preface, and reads the exception as deliberate: this was the race chosen by God, and Moses wished to sever it from the others by a special mark. The blessing does not descend to all his grandchildren indiscriminately but stays in one family; and although Eber's own descendants fell away from the true worship, so that God might justly have disinherited them, the benediction was not extinguished but only buried for a season until Abraham was called, in whose honour this dignity is ascribed to the name of Eber. Japheth is named alongside so the promise may be confirmed, that he shall dwell in the tents of Shem. Gill takes the same view of the whole book: for the sake of those whose father Shem is here called, this genealogy was written, and indeed all of Genesis, since the Hebrews sprang from Eber in Shem's line, among whom the church was kept and from whom the Messiah came. On the name Gill reports Jarchi's reading of Eber as beyond the river, Euphrates or Tigris, describing where Shem's posterity settled, but objects that this straitens them too much, since they lived on both sides, and cites Dr Hyde to show the word can cover both.

Henry finds two titles here rather than one. Shem is father of all the children of Eber, and Henry asks why he should be styled father of that great-grandson's line rather than of Arphaxad's or Salah's. His answer is that Abraham's seed both descended from Eber and were called Hebrews after him, so that Paul could count it a privilege to be a Hebrew of the Hebrews. He supposes Eber a man eminent for religion in a time of general apostasy, and thinks the holy tongue, called Hebrew from him, was probably kept in his family through the confusion of Babel as a token of God's favour, whence the professors of religion were called the children of Eber; and though the people were despised bond-slaves in Egypt when Moses wrote, it was an honour to be akin to them. The second title, brother of Japheth the elder, shows that although Shem is commonly put first he was not Noah's firstborn. Wesley, following Henry, asks why that should be part of Shem's description when it had been said already, and answers that it signifies the union of the Gentiles with the Jews, lest Japheth's seed be thought shut out. Clarke breaks with all of them, holding it much more likely that the Hebrews took their name not from Eber but from Abraham's passing over the Euphrates into Canaan, since the verb means to pass over.

Shem's sons are handled briskly. Clarke gives Elam to the Elamites near the Medes, Asshur to the province that became an empire, Lud to the Lydians of Asia Minor or a people at the confluence of the Euphrates and Tigris, and Aram to the Arameans afterwards called Syrians; on Arphaxad he can only offer Arrapachitis or Artaxata. Ellicott is blunter: the name at present defies all explanation. Keil and Delitzsch work through Aram's four sons with their usual caution, associating Uz with Ptolemy's Aesitae and the country of Job while calling the Aramaean connection mere conjecture, Hul with the Hylatae, Gether with the ancestor of two Arabian tribes, and Mash with Mount Masius above Nisibis. On Peleg they explain the name from the division of the earth's population after the tower, and note that his brother Joktan is called Kachtan by the Arabians and reckoned father of all their primitive tribes. Gill hears in Salah, a sending forth of waters, a memorial of the flood, given by Arphaxad, born two years after it, to his firstborn. Ellicott observes what the table then does: it turns to the Joktanite Arabs and omits the Hebrews, Eber's birth being recorded only to show where the primogeniture lay.
26:
Joktan's sons are traced mostly through Bochart, and Gill's notes show how thin the ground is there. Of Joktan the Arabic writers say he had thirty-one sons by one woman, all but two of whom left Arabia for India, while the Targum of Jonathan has him measure the earth with ropes, as though the first practiser of geometry. Hadoram looks like Ptolemy's Adramitae, but Bochart prefers Pliny's Drimati in the far east of Arabia, supporting himself with a promontory called Corodamum, which needs two letters transposed. Uzal keeps its name, R. Zacuth reporting that the Jews of Yaman so call the capital of that kingdom. For Obal, Bochart must carry the family across the straits of the Arabian Gulf into Arabia Troglodytice, where Pliny's Abalite bay preserves a trace of the name; and for Abimael his only foundation, Gill says plainly, is that Theophrastus mentions a place called Mali in spicy Arabia. Sheba is easier, naming the Sabaeans, whose country was famous for frankincense and whose tribes, on Pliny's account, stretched from the Arabian Gulf to the Persian. Ophir is hardest. If Joktan's sons went to India, Gill says, one is tempted to find him in the Ophir Solomon's ships sailed to; but that carries him too far from his brethren, so Bochart looks to an island named by Eupolemus.

The ends of their territory are no better fixed. Keil and Delitzsch say outright that Mesha is still unknown, rejecting as very improbable both Gesenius, who makes it Mesene on the Persian Gulf, and Knobel, who makes it a valley in northern Yemen; for Sephar they report the conjecture that it is the old Himyarite capital on the Indian Ocean, the mountain of the East being the mountain of incense further inland. Gill is more confident and more concrete. He takes Mesha for the Muza of Ptolemy and Pliny, a Red Sea port frequented by the merchants of Egypt and Ethiopia, and Zephar for the Saphar lying eastward at the foot of the range called Climax, to which those merchants went for myrrh and frankincense; the road between can be followed in Ptolemy's tables, and Pliny knew a Muza that the India trade did not use, only the dealers in frankincense. Clarke reports Calmet looking far further north, to Mount Masius in Mesopotamia on one side and mountains in Armenia or Media on the other.

Gill counts twenty-six names in Shem's branch and says at once there must have been many more, since no son of Elam, Asshur or Lud is named, only one of Arphaxad's and one of Salah's, two of Eber's and none of Peleg's. On the closing verse he insists the division was not immediate: it waited until the families had increased enough to form nations, until the days of Peleg and the building of the tower, and thence they peopled by degrees all the known parts of the world, and no doubt America, though how they passed there is unknown to us. He hears an echo of it in Pindar, who says that according to the ancients Jupiter and the immortals divided the earth, and speaks of one man with three sons dwelling apart. Ellicott draws an inference from the phrase after their generations: the Hebrew word suggests each family kept some record of its own descent, and that this table was compiled by comparing many such records. Keil reads the last clause as a bridge to the event that turned one race into many nations with different tongues. Clarke closes with an argument for the unity of mankind drawn from custom rather than names: reckoning by tens, counting time in weeks of seven days, keeping the seventh for religion, consecrating temples and altars, appointing places of refuge, giving a tenth of the produce to the altar, worshipping barefoot. Usages so widely shared, he argues, could only come from a common institution held before the dispersion.
